# Regional Adherence to Early Sepsis Management Bundle and Associated Mortality in Hong Kong Between 2009–2018

## Abstract

Longitudinal data are scarce on sepsis bundle adherence and associated survival at a country or regional level.

A population-based electronic health record database was leveraged to determine temporal trends in sepsis bundle adherence (empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic administration, blood culture collection, lactate measurement) on sepsis onset day and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prevalence. This study included all adult hospitalizations for community-acquired sepsis at 41 publicly funded hospitals in Hong Kong between 2009 and 2018. Generalized estimating equations were used to assess the association between full bundle adherence and its individual elements with hospital mortality.

Among 421 096 cases of community-acquired sepsis, the full bundle adherence rate increased from 0.2% in 2009 to 1.2% in 2018 (relative +18.9%/y, P < .001), with limited uptake of each element. The relative increase in empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics administration (+9.8%/y [95% CI, 8.3%–11.2%]) was faster than the AMR prevalence (+5.2%/y [95% CI, 3.6%–6.9%]). Full bundle adherence was associated with reduced mortality (adjusted odds ratio [ORadj], 0.75 [95% CI, .65–.86]). Blood culture collection was associated with reduced mortality (ORadj, 0.88 [95% CI, .83–.93]), while lactate measurement was associated only with reduced mortality in septic shock (ORadj, 0.85 [95% CI, .76–.94]). Broad-spectrum antibiotics was associated with reduced mortality (ORadj, 0.73 [95% CI, .56–.96]) when used appropriately in bacteremia from extended-spectrum beta-lactamase pathogens or methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

Basic sepsis care implementation remains challenging even in high-income settings. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic usage has outpaced AMR risk. Full sepsis bundle adherence was associated with improved survival, but empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics was associated with better survival only if used appropriately. Efforts should focus not only on ensuring bundle adherence but also on prioritizing the right treatments for the right patients.

Keywords: antibiotics, blood cultures, completion, compliance, lactate

## Abstract

Basic sepsis care implementation remains challenging even in high-income settings. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic usage outpaced antimicrobial resistance risk. Full bundle adherence was associated with improved sepsis survival, but empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics administration was associated with better survival only if used appropriately.

Sepsis is a major global health burden, and many countries have adopted national action plans that standardize provisions of sepsis care through management bundles [1–4]. However, a recent European survey study found that only 44% of participants reported consistent adherence to sepsis care bundles in their daily practice [5]. Real-world implementation of a sepsis bundle remains highly variable across countries and health care systems. For instance, emergency departments in South Korean tertiary centers achieve high 1-hour sepsis bundle adherence rates to blood culture collection (92%) and lactate measurement (81%) [6]. In contrast, an Ethiopian study reported that none of the patients with septic shock had these investigations performed within 1 hour of presentation at a teaching hospital [7]. Furthermore, very few studies have reported on longitudinal trends in real-world implementation of a sepsis bundle within a whole country or region [8–11].

Multiple studies, including one from Hong Kong, have shown that intervention programs improve sepsis bundle adherence [12–15]. But currently less than half of the emergency departments in public hospitals in Hong Kong have adopted guidelines on sepsis care, and none regularly audit bundle adherence [15]. Unlike in the United States, where reporting of sepsis bundle adherence is mandated through the national measure Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock Management Bundle (SEP-1), real-world bundle adherence across the whole region is currently unknown in Hong Kong [11].

Importantly, whether implementation of sepsis care bundles such as SEP-1 has translated to improved outcomes remains controversial [8, 9, 11, 16–20]. Systematic adoption of the whole SEP-1 bundle may carry risks of unintended consequences, such as increased use of unnecessarily broad antibiotics [21]. Although adequate empirical antibiotics is essential, use of overly broad antibiotics has been associated with increased mortality [21, 22].

The primary objective of this study was to assess the 10-year longitudinal trends in early sepsis management bundle adherence rates to empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic administration, blood culture collection, and lactate measurement for adults with community-acquired sepsis (CAS) in Hong Kong, a high-income region where protocolized sepsis care is not currently mandated. Secondary objectives were to evaluate associations between sepsis survival and both adherence to the full early sepsis management bundle and its individual elements.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Data Source

In this retrospective cohort study, a comprehensive population-wide electronic health record (EHR) database was leveraged to identify all adult (≥18 years old) hospitalizations for CAS at 41 publicly funded hospitals in Hong Kong between 1 April 2009 and 31 March 2019. The Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System (CDARS) is an EHR database that contains admission records, medication administration, operation records, laboratory and microbiological test results, and diagnosis and procedure codes from >90% of acute hospital care provided in Hong Kong [23]. The study calendar year started on 1 April and ended on 31 March in the following year to match with the statistical years of public hospitals in Hong Kong. Each hospital episode started with admission to a public hospital and ended upon discharge home (alive) or death. Interhospital transfers were considered continuous hospitalizations. This study was approved by The Joint Chinese University of Hong Kong–New Territories East Cluster Clinical Research Ethics Committee (2019.214) and other local ethics committees.

### CAS Definition

A validated EHR sepsis surveillance definition based on objective clinical data was used to identify cases of CAS [23, 24]. Sepsis was defined by clinical markers of presumed infection (at least 1 microbiological test and antibiotic administration for ≥4 days) and concurrent acute organ dysfunction (delta Sequential Organ Failure Assessment [ΔSOFA] score ≥2) per Sepsis-3 criteria [25]. Cultures taken for infection control surveillance were excluded (Figure 1, Supplementary Table 1). Sepsis onset date was defined by the date of the first microbiological culture (index culture), and cases were designated as CAS if all criteria were met within the first 3 calendar days of hospitalization [23]. CAS with septic shock (CASS) was defined as sepsis with use of inotropes or vasopressors within the first 3 calendar days of hospitalization.

*Figure 1.: Study flowchart. Culture samples positive for coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species from any site or Enterococcus species isolated from respiratory samples within 3 calendar days of hospital admission were excluded since it is difficult to define true infection from contaminant. Cases of community-acquired sepsis that did not receive antibiotics within 3 calendar days of hospital admission were excluded. ESBL, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase; ICU, intensive care unit; MRSA, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.*

### Estimated SOFA Score

A previous study provides a detailed explanation on calculation of the SOFA score based on objective clinical data—laboratory results including bilirubin, creatinine, platelet, Glasgow Coma Scale, and PaO2/FiO2, as well as medication records—and diagnosis/procedure codes [23]. ΔSOFA score was calculated by the difference between the highest SOFA score obtained within ±2 calendar days of sepsis onset date and the prehospital SOFA score. Missing laboratory data were assumed to be normal [26].

### Sepsis Care Bundle and Antimicrobial Resistance

Protocolized sepsis care and bundle adherence are currently not mandated in Hong Kong public hospitals, and less than half of the emergency departments have established guidelines for sepsis management [15]. Hong Kong does not currently have a coordinated action plan on sepsis. We assessed the adherence to 3 core elements of an early sepsis management bundle for CAS and CASS: ≥1 broad-spectrum antibiotic administered, ≥2 blood cultures collected, and ≥1 lactate measurement. We focused on adherence to the full bundle and its individual elements within the same calendar day of sepsis onset for 2 reasons. First, time stamps of blood culture collection and lactate measurement in the CDARS were available in hours, but antibiotic administration time stamp data were limited to calendar days. Second, clinical recognition of sepsis and the duration of sepsis prior to presentation are imprecise [11, 27, 28]. Sensitivity analysis was performed by considering the sepsis bundle adherence rate within 2 calendar days of the sepsis onset day (same day and next calendar day) to mitigate bias against patients admitted in late hours on the sepsis onset day. Intravenous fluid administration was not assessed since intravenous fluid volume data are not captured in the CDARS.

Empirical administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics was defined as administration an antipseudomonal beta-lactam or antibiotic with anti–methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus activity (Supplementary Table 2) within the same calendar day of sepsis onset [11 ]. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was present when there was ≥1 of the following pathogens isolated in cultures within 3 days of hospitalization: extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL), methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA), carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (Supplementary Methods).

### Statistical Analysis

Annual adherence rates to the full sepsis bundle and its individual elements were determined for CAS and CASS, as were AMR prevalence and mortality risk. Trends in annual adherence rates were also assessed according to the ΔSOFA score and ward setting (general ward or intensive care unit). Overall sepsis bundle adherence rates were compared between teaching and nonteaching hospitals. Trends in annual rates of adherence to administration of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics were compared with AMR prevalence in CAS and 4 subgroups: CAS with positive bacterial cultures, CAS with bacteremia, CASS with positive bacterial culture, and CASS with bacteremia (Supplementary Methods).

Exponential regression was used to model the relative annual change of rate/proportion estimates. Mortality from sepsis upon hospital discharge was defined as all-cause hospital mortality. All cases were followed up until discharge home or death. Patients were assumed to have survived the hospital episode if the discharge status could not be retrieved (0.01%).

Generalized estimating equations (GEEs) with binomial family, logit link function, independent working correlation structure, and adjustment for clustering effect were used to model the association (adjusted odds ratio [ORadj]) between full sepsis bundle adherence or individual elements and mortality, with adjustments for covariates. Only the most recent hospital admission of each patient was used in this mortality analysis to reflect the most current data on mortality outcomes as possible. To minimize bias due to delay in sepsis recognition, only patients treated for sepsis on the day of hospital admission were included (index culture performed on the day of hospital presentation) [23]. Selection of covariates such as ΔSOFA, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and others was based on associations with mortality according to a directed acyclic graph (Supplementary Figure 1A and 1B). A clustering effect was modeled by individual hospitals within each calendar year to account for annual changes to hospital-level organizational factors such as staffing and clinical services. A final cohort of 202 005 unique patients with CAS who were treated for sepsis on the day of hospital admission were included for GEE mortality analyses (Figure 1).

Sensitivity analyses of GEE modeling for the association between full bundle adherence or individual elements and mortality were performed in 4 subgroups:

- CASS: since patients with septic shock may receive the greatest benefit from adherence to sepsis bundles

- CAS with bacteremia: to evaluate bundle effects in confirmed bacterial sepsis rather than the original analysis, which assessed all patients treated for suspected CAS, since the latter includes patients who may not have underlying infection and thus may not benefit from sepsis bundles

- CAS with bacteremia from ESBL pathogens or MRSA: to evaluate the overall effects of any empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (not specifically targeting ESBL pathogens or MRSA) in patients with sepsis from resistant organisms

- Appropriate use of empirical anti-ESBL and anti-MRSA antibiotics in CAS with bacteremia from ESBL pathogens or MRSA: to determine the association of early appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics and mortality risk

For broad-spectrum antibiotic administration to be considered appropriate in CAS cases with bacteremia from ESBL pathogens or MRSA, patients must have received either an anti-ESBL antibiotic if they had ESBL gram-negative bacteremia or anti-MRSA if they had MRSA bacteremia within the first day of hospital admission. Broad-spectrum antibiotics use was inappropriate if any anti-ESBL or anti-MRSA antibiotic was administered to patients without either type of resistant organism.

All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.2.2), and analytic figures were created by the ggplot2 package. For all statistical tests, P < .05 (2-sided) was considered statistically significant without Bonferroni adjustment.

## RESULTS

### Characteristics of Cohort

A total of 421 096 hospitalizations with CAS were identified during the study decade (Figure 1). The median age was 77 years (IQR, 64–85), and 41.5% of patients were female (Table 1). The most common infection site was respiratory (36.3%), and overall mortality was 21.6%. Bacterial pathogens were found in 42.2% of CAS cases. The most common bacterial pathogens were Escherichia coli (34.3%), Klebsiella (13.2%), and S aureus (9.7%; Supplementary Table 3A and 3B, Supplementary Figure 2).

### Sepsis Bundle Adherence

Adherence rates to full sepsis bundle for CAS and CASS increased from 0.2% in 2009 to 1.2% in 2018 (relative +18.9%/y [95% CI, 15.2%–22.6%]; P < .001) and from 0.6% in 2009 to 5.6% in 2018 (relative +27.9%/y [95% CI, 18.9%–37.7%]; P < .001), respectively (Figure 2A, Supplementary Table 4). Blood culture collection rates for CAS and CASS gradually increased from 6.4% in 2009 to 7.8% in 2018 (relative +2.2%/y [95% CI, 0.9%–3.4%]; P = .004) and from 14.5% in 2009 to 18.0% in 2018 (relative +2.3%/y [95% CI, 0.6%–4.2%]; P = .02; Figure 2C). Lactate measurement rates in CAS and CASS also increased from 2.8% in 2009 to 12.1% in 2018 (relative +17.0%/y [95% CI, 14.1%–20.0%]; P < .001) and from 5.2% in 2009 to 28.8% in 2018 (relative +20.9%/y [95% CI, 16.6%–25.3%]; P < .001) in 2018 (Figure 2D).

Proportions of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics administration and AMR prevalence in CAS were 19.6% and 11.0% in 2018, respectively (Figure 2B, Supplementary Table 4). The relative rate of increase in empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics administration (+9.8%/y [95% CI, 8.3%–11.2%]; P < .001) was faster than that of AMR prevalence (+5.2%/y [95% CI, 3.6%–6.9%]; P < .001). These trends were similar for CAS with positive bacterial cultures, CAS with bacteremia, CASS with positive bacterial cultures, and CASS with bacteremia (Supplementary Figures 3 and 4, Supplementary Table 5).

Trends in bundle adherence were similar when adherence was assessed within 2 calendar days of sepsis onset (Supplementary Figure 5, Supplementary Table 6). Overall full sepsis bundle adherence rates were higher in 2 teaching hospitals for CAS (1.4% vs 0.6%, P < .001) and CASS (8.4% vs 3.3%, P < .001) when compared with nonteaching hospitals during the study period (Supplementary Table 7). Adherence rates to the full sepsis bundle and its individual elements were correlated with severity of sepsis and consistently higher in intensive care units than wards over time and across all severity of sepsis (Figure 3, Supplementary Figure 6A and 6B).

### Association Between Bundle Adherence and Mortality

Adherence to full sepsis bundle was associated with improved survival as compared with nonadherence in CAS (ORadj, 0.75 [95% CI, .65–.86]; P < .001) and CASS (ORadj, 0.80 [95% CI, .68–.94]; P = .007) on multivariate analysis (Figure 4, Supplementary Table 8A). Blood culture collection was associated with reduced mortality risk in CAS (ORadj, 0.88 [95% CI, .83–.93]; P < .001) and CASS (ORadj, 0.77 [95% CI, .70–.86]; P < .001). In contrast, lactate measurement was associated only with improved survival in CASS (ORadj, 0.85 [95% CI, .76–.94]; P = .002; Supplementary Table 8B).

*Figure 4.: Association between sepsis bundle adherence and mortality. Note that only the most recent hospital admission and treatment for sepsis on the day of admission were included for each patient. A logarithmic scale is used on the x-axis of the forest plot. The 4 subgroups included CASS, bacteremia, bacteremia from ESBL pathogens or MRSA, and early appropriate anti-ESBL or anti-MRSA antibiotics in CAS from ESBL pathogens or MRSA bacteremia. CAS, community-acquired sepsis; CASS, community-acquired septic shock; ESBL, extended spectrum beta-lactamase; MRSA, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.*

Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics administration was not associated with mortality in CASS (ORadj, 1.05 [95% CI, .97–1.12]; P = .24). However, it was associated with higher mortality risk among all patients treated for CAS (ORadj, 1.65 [95% CI, 1.58–1.72]; P < .001) and CAS with bacteremia (ORadj, 1.55 [95% CI, 1.45–1.66]; P < .001). Even in CAS cases with bacteremia from ESBL pathogens or MRSA, administering empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics without specifically targeting ESBL pathogens or MRSA was still associated with harm (ORadj, 1.26 [95% CI, 1.07–1.48]; P = .005). Only empirical administration of appropriate anti-ESBL or anti-MRSA broad-spectrum antibiotics was associated with improved survival in CAS from bacteremia due to ESBL pathogens or MRSA (ORadj, 0.73 [95% CI, .56–.96]; P = .02).

## DISCUSSION

In this 10-year population cohort of 421 096 cases with CAS, bundle adherence rates for empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics administration, blood culture collection, and lactate measurement increased over time but remained very low in a high-income region where protocolized care was not mandated. Concerningly, trends in use of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic outpaced the growth in AMR prevalence. Although adherence to full sepsis bundle was associated with improved survival from sepsis and septic shock, administration of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics was associated only with improved survival if its use was appropriate.

Apart from a study from Japan, this is the only study that evaluated temporal trends in sepsis care bundle adherence for an entire region in Asia [10]. Although adherence rates to blood culture collection and lactate measurements for septic shock in Hong Kong are increasing, they remained at only 18.0% and 28.8% in 2019, respectively. These are exceedingly low adherence rates when compared with rates >80% reported from other Asian high-income countries and regions, such as Japan and South Korea [6, 10]. This study highlights that implementation of basic sepsis care remains challenging even in high-income settings.

Several strategies may be used to increase sepsis care bundle adherence. First, direct sepsis care education for nurses and physicians translates to immediate positive knowledge outcomes and higher sepsis care bundle adherence [29, 30]. Second, implementation of departmental or hospital-wide sepsis care protocols can improve sepsis bundle adherence [12–14, 30]. Importantly, structured performance feedback that targets deficiencies in protocol adherence facilitates successful implementation [31, 32]. Third, national initiatives such as SEP-1 in the United States, which mandates reporting of sepsis bundle adherence for hospital reimbursement, has been shown to increase protocol adherence [11]. Fourth, automated electronic alert systems can effectively enhance adherence to sepsis care bundles [33].

Our data suggest that full sepsis care bundle adherence was associated with improved mortality in sepsis and septic shock. However, whether benefit is derived from adherence to the full bundle or specific bundle elements requires further consideration. Blood culture collection has been associated with improved sepsis survival in multiple studies [8, 9, 18]. Our data support the guidance from the Surviving Sepsis Campaign and Infectious Diseases Society of America to routinely obtain blood cultures for all patients with suspected sepsis to detect causative bacterial pathogens and facilitate attainment of appropriate antibiotics [28, 34]. In contrast, the value of routine lactate measurement for patients with suspected sepsis is more controversial [8, 9, 11, 16–18]. Lactate is widely used as a surrogate marker of tissue perfusion, and our study suggests that lactate measurement may be more useful in septic shock than in sepsis without shock. It should be emphasized that it is a personalized resuscitative response to lactate rather than the mere measurement of lactate alone that may improve septic shock survival [9, 35].

Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics are recommended to treat sepsis, but wide implementation of this strategy has not been consistently shown to improve outcomes [8, 9, 11, 16–20, 34]. Moreover, this approach may have undesirable consequences at an individual and population level [22, 28, 36]. Concerningly, our findings reveal that, similar to trends in the United States, the use of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis in Hong Kong has risen at a rate far exceeding the increase in AMR risk [21]. Of note, administration of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis without shock was associated with potential harm in our study. While this association should be interpreted with caution due to possible residual confounding—such as greater illness severity, prompting broader empiric therapy—other studies have similarly reported worse outcomes with unnecessarily broad antibiotic use [36–38]. It is unclear why independent studies have found that inappropriately broad empirical therapy is associated with higher mortality, but greater subsequent risk of AMR, Clostridioides difficile infection, and disruption of host microbiome may be contributing factors [39–41]. Moreover, most prior evaluations of sepsis bundle adherence have focused solely on the timing of antibiotic administration, without accounting for AMR data or assessing the appropriateness of antibiotic selection in relation to patient outcomes [8, 9, 11, 16–20].

In contrast, we assessed the timing and appropriateness of broad-spectrum antibiotics by evaluating individual-level microbiological data on the presence of multidrug-resistant organisms. Use of empirical anti-ESBL or anti-MRSA antibiotics was associated only with better sepsis survival when used appropriately in patients with bacteremia from ESBL pathogens or MRSA. Our study underscores that it is the combination of early and appropriately broad antibiotics administration that should be the cornerstone of sepsis management. But to achieve this, rapid pathogen and resistance detection tools are critical in guiding the initiation and spectrum of antibiotic therapy. Until such tools are widely available, antibiotics stewardship is imperative to curb the global rise in AMR and prevent individual harm from exposure to unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics [42, 43].

Key strengths of our study include the use of objective data to define sepsis and quantify severity of organ dysfunction, the longitudinal territory-wide cohort with minimal loss to follow-up, and the comprehensive modeling of covariates in mortality risk analyses. There are also several key limitations. First, similar to other large-scale studies on sepsis bundles, we were unable to assess intravenous fluid therapy because this was not reliably captured in our EHR database [11, 19]. Second, reasons why sepsis bundle adherence rates have changed over time were not assessed. Third, the association between bundle adherence and mortality does not prove causation, as it may simply reflect higher-quality provider care in a region where bundle adherence is low. However, timely blood culture collection and lactate measurement may improve sepsis outcomes by guiding the selection of targeted antibiotic therapy and stratifying patients for hemodynamic monitoring and resuscitation. Fourth, we did not determine whether blood cultures were collected prior to antibiotic administration since time stamp data on antibiotics was limited to calendar days. Fifth, we did not assess sepsis bundle adherence in private hospitals, although our study did capture >90% of acute care provided in Hong Kong.

## CONCLUSION

Implementation of basic sepsis care remains challenging even in high-income settings. Temporal trends in use of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics outpaced the growth in actual AMR risk. Adherence to the full sepsis bundle was associated with improved survival from sepsis and septic shock, but administration of empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics was associated with better survival only if used appropriately. These findings suggest that efforts to improve sepsis care should focus not only on ensuring bundle adherence but also on prioritizing the right treatments for the right patients.
